analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection queues appear in this snapshot — ERCOT, NYISO, SPP, MISO, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.1 million megawatts of generation and storage projects somewhere between study and commissioning as of August 30, 2026. These are requests to connect, not built capacity, and the operators' own scope notes make clear the figures are not directly comparable: ERCOT counts projects from study through commissioning, CAISO excludes completed and withdrawn projects, SPP counts withdrawn requests separately, and so on. ERCOT's Texas queue alone stands at roughly 440,000 MW across 1,797 requests, with solar at about 152,000 MW, storage at about 161,000 MW, and gas at about 77,000 MW leading the fuel mix there; SPP shows nearly 200,000 MW across 1,078 requests, with wind at roughly 65,000 MW and storage at about 53,000 MW alongside gas at about 47,000 MW; MISO's roughly 88,000 MW across 3,827 requests skews heavily solar; and CAISO's roughly 72,000 MW across 265 active requests is dominated by storage at nearly 47,000 MW.

Storage and gas interconnection requests are the figures that readers focused on AI data centers should watch most carefully, because both fuel types track dispatchable, around-the-clock load rather than weather-dependent generation. Across the five queues, storage totals roughly 267,000 MW — with ERCOT accounting for about 161,000 MW, SPP about 53,000 MW, CAISO about 47,000 MW, and MISO about 6,000 MW — while gas totals roughly 160,000 MW spread across all five operators. The queue totals are planned generation and storage waiting to connect, not data center demand itself, but a sustained rise in storage and gas requests in the same geographies where data center campuses are clustering is a meaningful directional signal. The EIA commercial electricity sales figures for June 2026 offer a separate, non-comparable lens: Texas reported roughly 15,754 gigawatt-hours of commercial sales that month at an average of $8.66 per megawatt-hour, Virginia reported roughly 7,771 gigawatt-hours at $10.99, and California reported roughly 10,025 gigawatt-hours at $27.33, though EIA's own scope note is explicit that data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, making this a proxy for their load rather than a direct measurement.

These are snapshots from a single day, and interconnection queues are living documents in which projects enter, withdraw, and change status continuously, so the most informative next step will be comparing the August 2026 storage and gas subtotals in ERCOT and SPP against the figures that appear in those operators' next monthly releases to see whether the pipeline is growing, shrinking, or shifting fuel mix.
